reference.source: Miller's Review of Orthopaedics / Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Usually caused by a direct fall onto the point of the shoulder with the arm adducted
Graded by the Rockwood classification (I-VI) according to acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular ligament disruption and clavicle displacement
Types I and II are sprains without significant displacement; type III shows complete separation with a visible step; types IV-VI are severe displaced patterns
Tenderness localises to the AC joint, with a palpable step and a positive cross-body adduction test
Weighted stress radiographs are rarely needed; bilateral views help gauge coracoclavicular distance
Most types I-III are managed non-operatively, while types IV-VI and some high-demand type III injuries are considered for surgery
Late AC joint osteoarthritis or distal clavicle osteolysis can follow, particularly in weight-trainers
reference.pathophysiology: A downward force on the acromion sprains then sequentially disrupts the acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular (conoid and trapezoid) ligaments and the deltotrapezial fascia. Progressive ligament failure allows the clavicle to displace superiorly (or posteriorly/inferiorly in higher grades) relative to the acromion, producing the characteristic deformity and loss of the strut function of the clavicle.
additionalInvestigations: Bilateral AP radiographs with comparison of coracoclavicular distance
Axillary lateral view to detect posterior displacement, and a Zanca view to assess the AC joint and coracoclavicular distance
MRI where associated rotator cuff or labral injury is suspected
Clinical grading with cross-body adduction testing
redFlags: Skin tenting or threatened skin over a severely displaced clavicle
Posterior displacement with mediastinal or neurovascular compromise
reference.prognosis: Low-grade injuries recover well with rehabilitation, sometimes leaving a painless cosmetic bump; high-grade or operatively treated injuries generally regain good function, though some develop persistent AC joint pain or arthritis.
pitfalls: Misclassifying a type III as lower grade by omitting an axillary view that reveals posterior displacement
Operating routinely on type III injuries when many do well non-operatively
Overlooking a concomitant distal clavicle fracture or cuff tear
Attributing persistent pain solely to the separation when AC arthritis has developed
references: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
management: Non-operative management for Rockwood types I to III: a period of sling immobilisation, analgesia and early mobilisation
Simple analgesics or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs with ice for acute pain control
Physiotherapy-led graduated rehabilitation to restore scapular control, range of motion and shoulder-girdle strength
Surgical stabilisation with coracoclavicular ligament reconstruction for types IV to VI and selected high-demand type III injuries
Graduated return to sport or heavy activity once pain-free with restored strength and range
Surveillance for persistent acromioclavicular joint pain or post-traumatic arthritis, managed with corticosteroid injection or later distal clavicle excision
Orthopaedic or sports-medicine referral for high-grade or refractory injuries
